content: Soft tissue therapy, commonly referred to as STT, involves the evaluation, treatment, and management of injuries, pain, and dysfunction affecting the soft tissues, particularly within the neuromusculoskeletal system. This therapy is typically administered by licensed healthcare professionals such as chiropractors, massage therapists, physical therapists, and some osteopathic and naturopathic doctors, as well as other manual therapy providers. Repetitive strain injuries (RSIs), also known as cumulative trauma disorders (CTDs), are increasingly common and represent a significant portion of disability and impairment cases. Healthcare professionals who provide soft tissue therapy are generally well-versed in anatomy, physiology, pathology, pathophysiology, biomechanics, functional anatomy, and tactile/palpatory and functional movement assessments. Postural and Functional Assessments Patients presenting with specific complaints typically undergo a series of assessments tailored to their symptoms and clinical presentation. These assessments aim to gather detailed information about the condition of the patient’s soft tissues and help identify the most likely cause of their pain or injury. Evaluations may include assessments of posture, biomechanics, range of motion, and the nervous system, among other factors. If the findings suggest a condition or symptoms beyond the practitioner’s expertise or scope of practice, the patient will be referred to an appropriate healthcare professional. Treatment Strategies The specific treatment approach for pain, injury, or dysfunction is determined based on the results of the assessments. A variety of techniques may be employed to achieve optimal outcomes. The effectiveness of treatment often depends on the practitioner’s skill level and their understanding of anatomy, physiology, and dysfunction. Advanced skills allow for more precise and intricate treatment applications. Manual Techniques Trigger Point Techniques: These are used to alleviate myofascial trigger points, which are hyperirritable spots in the muscle or fascia. Myofascial Therapy: This technique targets the muscle and fascial systems to improve flexibility and mobility of connective tissues. It also helps mobilize fibrous adhesions and reduces the severity and sensitivity of scarring caused by injury or surgery. Massage Techniques: Often referred to as Swedish massage in traditional contexts, these broad-handed techniques aim to reduce swelling and inflammation as part of soft tissue therapy. Cross Friction: This technique generates heat to mobilize adhesions between fascial layers, muscles, and other soft tissues. It may also provoke an inflammatory response that focuses healing on the injured area, particularly in tendon pathologies. Sustained Pressure (Ischaemic/Digital Pressure): This method is used to relieve hypertonic (tight) areas within muscles and fascia. Other Techniques: Methods such as Active Release Therapy, Myofascial Release, and Deep Tissue Massage often combine elements of the above techniques. These approaches, whether used individually or in combination, may address pain, injury, or dysfunction. However, it is misleading to claim that any single technique will consistently resolve a specific condition. Stretching Static Stretching: This approach aims to alleviate excessively tight muscles by holding them in a lengthened position. PNF Stretching (Proprioceptive Neuromuscular Facilitation): This technique is used to decrease muscle tone in hypertonic muscles or muscle groups. It is also commonly employed to address delayed onset muscle soreness (DOMS). Originating over a century ago in the field of osteopathy, PNF stretching can alter joint restrictions and improve joint range of motion by modifying the length of local musculature. Exercise Prescription Dysfunctional soft tissues are often either too short and tight or too long and weak. Based on assessment findings, some patients may be prescribed specific exercises to strengthen or activate particular muscles or muscle groups. These exercises are designed to restore balance and functionality to the affected tissues. Taping Soft tissue practitioners and musculoskeletal specialists frequently use therapeutic taping or strapping techniques to relieve pressure on swollen, injured tissues, modify muscle firing patterns, or provide support during the healing process. These techniques enhance lymphatic fluid exchange and facilitate the body’s natural healing mechanisms. After soft tissue injuries caused by sports activities, overexertion, or repetitive strain injuries (e.g., carpal tunnel syndrome), swelling can impede blood flow to the injured area, slowing the healing process. Trained specialists effectively use elastic taping to reduce pressure from swollen tissues and improve blood circulation to the injured fascia and muscle mass. Advice As part of a comprehensive treatment plan, patients are often encouraged to actively participate in their recovery to achieve optimal outcomes. This may involve attending scheduled appointments, performing prescribed home exercises, making dietary adjustments, or engaging in self-massage techniques.
